patterns: what can you help me with
response: SkillGapPath figures out what you already know in a skill using a short quiz, finds the gap between that and your goal, and then recommends courses, videos and a roadmap starting exactly from where you left off — not from the basics you already know.

patterns: why do i need to take a quiz
why do i have to answer questions first
response: The cold-start quiz solves the 'new user' problem: since we don't know your skill level yet, we ask a couple of quick questions per topic. Your answers build your initial skill profile so recommendations don't start from zero if you already know the basics.

The roadmap is built from a prerequisite graph: each topic depends on the ones before it. 'Mastered' means you've shown you know it, 'ready' means its prerequisites are done so you can start it now, and 'locked' means you need to finish something else first.

The 'AI match' percentage comes from a logistic regression model that estimates how likely you are to complete a course, based on how well your current skill level fits the course's difficulty and whether you've met its prerequisites.

patterns: how do i keep my streak
response: Your streak counts consecutive days you've done something on the platform — like submitting a quiz or a topic test. Do at least one activity each day to keep it going; missing a day resets your current streak, but your longest streak is always saved.

patterns: how do i translate the video
response: Below each video there's a language dropdown — pick your language and the transcript will be fetched and translated, then shown as text under the video. If a specific video doesn't have captions available, you can still use YouTube's own CC/gear icon on the player itself to translate subtitles.

A variable is a named container that stores a value in memory. Python's core data types include int (whole numbers), float (decimals), str (text), and bool (True/False). Python figures out the type automatically based on the value you assign.

Control flow decides which code runs and how many times. `if/elif/else` picks a branch based on a condition. `for` loops repeat over a sequence a known number of times; `while` loops repeat as long as a condition stays true.
A function is a reusable block of code defined with `def name(parameters):` that can take inputs and return an output. This keeps code organized and avoids repeating yourself.

Object-Oriented Programming organizes code around 'objects' created from 'classes' (blueprints). Inheritance lets one class reuse and extend another class's behavior, so you avoid rewriting shared logic.
A Python list is an ordered, resizable collection that can hold mixed types, accessed by index starting at 0. It's Python's built-in 'array'-like structure.
JavaScript is the language that makes web pages interactive. `let` and `const` are modern, block-scoped ways to declare variables (preferred over the older, function-scoped `var`).

Flexbox and CSS Grid are layout systems. Flexbox arranges items along a single row or column and is great for aligning things; Grid arranges items in a full two-dimensional row-and-column layout, better for whole-page structure.

The backend is the server-side part of an app: it handles requests, talks to the database, and returns data. A REST API is a common way to structure that communication using URLs and HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.

Machine learning is building models that learn patterns from data instead of following hardcoded rules. Supervised learning learns from labeled examples (input + correct answer); unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels, like grouping similar items together.

Precision asks: of everything the model predicted positive, how much was actually correct? Recall asks: of everything that was actually positive, how much did the model find? F1 score is the harmonic mean of the two, useful when you need a single balanced number instead of two separate ones.

NumPy provides fast array-based numerical computing in Python. Pandas builds on top of that to give you DataFrames — table-like structures great for loading, cleaning, and analyzing labeled data such as CSV files.

Big O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory use grows as the input size grows. O(1) means constant time regardless of input size, O(n) means it grows linearly, and O(n^2) means it grows much faster (like nested loops over the same data).

A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node points to the next one. Unlike arrays, elements aren't stored contiguously in memory, so inserting at the front is fast (O(1)) but random access is slow (O(n)) since you have to walk the chain.

Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges them back together in order — reliably O(n log n). Quicksort picks a 'pivot', partitions elements around it, then recursively sorts each side — usually fast in practice, also O(n log n) on average.

Dynamic programming solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing (memoizing) each subproblem's answer so it's never recomputed. It works when a problem has 'optimal substructure' — the best overall solution is built from the best solutions to its subproblems.

patterns: what is a binary search tree
response: A binary search tree keeps every node's left subtree smaller and right subtree larger than itself. That structure lets you search, insert, and delete in O(log n) time on average, since each comparison rules out half the remaining tree.

BFS (breadth-first search) explores a graph level by level using a queue, good for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS (depth-first search) goes as deep as possible down one path before backtracking, using a stack (often via recursion).

patterns: how do i write a select statement
response: SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to relational databases. A basic query looks like `SELECT column FROM table WHERE condition;` — SELECT picks columns, FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows.

A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables; LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matches from the right (with NULLs where there's no match).

Normalization organizes database tables to reduce redundant data and avoid update anomalies, by splitting data into related tables. Each 'normal form' (1NF, 2NF, 3NF...) adds a stricter rule, like requiring atomic column values or removing indirect (transitive) dependencies.

patterns: what does an operating system do
response: An operating system manages a computer's hardware and provides services to programs — scheduling the CPU, managing memory, and handling files and devices. The kernel is its core, running with the most privileged access to hardware.

A process is a running program with its own memory space. A thread is a smaller unit of execution *within* a process — multiple threads in the same process share memory, which makes them lighter-weight than separate processes but requires care to avoid conflicts.

A deadlock happens when two or more processes each hold a resource the other needs and neither can proceed — like two people each waiting for the other to hand over a tool. It requires four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

The OSI model splits network communication into 7 layers, from Physical (raw bits/cables) up through Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, to Application (what your browser talks to). Each layer only needs to know how to talk to the layers directly above and below it.

patterns: what is the three way handshake
response: TCP is a reliable, connection-based protocol — it guarantees ordered delivery via a 'three-way handshake' (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before sending data. UDP skips that reliability for speed, which suits things like video streaming where a dropped packet matters less than a delay.

DNS translates human-friendly domain names (like example.com) into IP addresses computers actually use to route traffic. HTTP is the protocol browsers use to request and receive web pages; HTTPS adds encryption via TLS on top of it.

patterns: how do i start system design
response: System design is about planning how a large software system's components fit together to meet requirements like scale, reliability, and speed. It usually starts with clarifying requirements, then sketching the high-level architecture before diving into specifics like databases or caching.

A load balancer sits in front of multiple servers and distributes incoming requests across them, so no single server gets overwhelmed. Common strategies include round robin (rotate evenly) and least-connections (send to the least busy server).

Caching stores a copy of frequently-needed data somewhere faster to access (like memory) so you don't repeat expensive work every time. The tricky part is cache invalidation — knowing when cached data is stale and needs refreshing.

A monolith is one large application handling everything together. Microservices split that into small, independently deployable services that each own one responsibility and talk to each other over the network — more flexible to scale and deploy, but more complex to coordinate.

Git is a version control system that tracks changes to your files over time. `git init` starts tracking a folder, `git add` stages changes, and `git commit` saves a snapshot of those staged changes with a message describing what changed.

A branch is an independent line of development, letting you work on a feature without touching the main codebase. Merging brings those changes back together; a merge conflict happens when the same lines were changed differently on both branches and Git needs you to pick which version wins.

A pull request (PR) proposes your branch's changes for review before merging into the main branch. Teammates can comment, request changes, or approve it — it's the standard way collaborative teams review code on GitHub.
